title: The pencil maker's son
hookLine: Thoreau worked in his family's pencil business and as a surveyor
last: LOOK AS IF FOR THE FIRST TIME.

cards: A new block begins today, and its man comes in carrying a pencil. In Concord, the Thoreau family ran a small business making pencils.
One of the sons, Henry, worked in it: grinding, mixing, shaping, getting the lead to write smooth and even.

Later he earned money another way too, walking the fields and woodlots around town with a chain and a compass, as a land surveyor. You met Henry David Thoreau early on this path, going to live in a cabin by a pond.
This path will get back there. But it starts where he started: at a workbench, with dusty hands, doing ordinary work.

teach.b: First, the work was real. Thoreau didn't just help in the family shop. By the usual account he put real thought into making the pencils better, and the family's pencils earned a good name.
Ordinary work, done with care. Second, the story Emerson told.
After Thoreau died, Emerson spoke about his friend and told this: once Henry had made a pencil as good as the best, friends congratulated him on his future, and he said he would never make another.
Why do again, he asked, what he had already done once? Some hear arrogance in that. Others hear a man who refused to let his whole life become one job, even a job he was good at.
Third, the surveyor. Thoreau measured property lines for his neighbors. It paid the bills, and it put him out in the land he loved, pacing the edges of fields and woods.
His work and his walking were never quite separate. Fourth, the thread to his later writing.
In Walden he wrote, "Every man is tasked to make his life, even in its details, worthy of the contemplation of his most elevated and critical hour."
Even in its details: a pencil, a property line, a shelf, a spreadsheet. For Thoreau, ordinary work wasn't the opposite of a spiritual life. Done well, and kept in its place, it was part of one.

how: Readers of Thoreau often begin with his working life, the family pencil business and his surveying, as a way into his idea that ordinary work, done with care, belongs to a deliberate life.

games.q: what does “the pencil maker's son” mean?
o: a Concord craftsman Emerson praised in one essay
a nickname for any careful, plain-spoken writer
Henry David Thoreau, who made pencils and surveyed land

s: Thoreau never held an ordinary job
he worked in the family pencil business and as a land surveyor.
the story of never making another pencil comes from Emerson
Emerson told it when he spoke about his friend after Thoreau died.

games.q: you're Henry. you've just made a pencil as good as the best, and friends say your fortune is made. what do you do?
o: build the business and make them by the crate.
say you'll never make another; why do again what you've done once?
sell the method to a bigger company.
games.why: in Emerson's telling, Henry said he would never make another pencil. some hear arrogance; others hear a man who wouldn't let one job become his whole life.

practice: Recall something you finished recently, a meal, a report, a repair, a made bed, and turn it over slowly, the way a pencil maker might turn a pencil. Look for the one detail nobody else would notice, with no verdict and no scolding.
Then ask Thoreau's question of it, would this stand in my best hour, and let the answer be honest and kind.

wordCard.voice: The pencil maker's son. Henry David Thoreau, who worked in his family's pencil business and as a surveyor before he was ever a well-known writer. Today's word.
